catalog_locator: Gramática chinanteca sec. 5.1 'Derivación por medio de prefijos', p. 254. Tone / ballistic-accent description: 'Los tonos', pp. xi-xii.
catalog_quote: El prefijo läˉ- se combina con un adjetivo y lo convierte en un verbo intransitivo. Es posible que el verbo laꜗ ser, suceder sea la fuente de este prefijo. Puesto que el acento básico de la palabra siempre aparece en la última sílaba, la vocal del prefijo está en una posición que no se acentúa, lo que permite que la pronunciación de la vocal a se “afloje”, es decir, se pronuncie como la vocal ä. [examples:] lle̱ey̱ꜘ ADJ AN enojado / dsaˉläˉlle̱ey̱ꜘ VI AN enojar

Puesto que el acento básico de la palabra siempre aparece en la última sílaba, la vocal del prefijo está en una posición que no se acentúa, lo que permite que la pronunciación de la vocal a se "afloje", es decir, se pronuncie como la vocal ä.
new_statements.translation: The prefix läˉ- combines with an adjective and turns it into an intransitive verb. It is possible that the verb laꜗ 'to be, to happen' is the source of this prefix. Since the basic accent of the word always appears on the last syllable, the vowel of the prefix is in a position that is not accented, which allows the pronunciation of the vowel a to 'loosen', that is, to be pronounced as the vowel ä.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (the 'acento básico de la palabra') always falls on the final syllable, which is the root/stem syllable; the tense, directional and derivational prefixes (miˉ-, läˉ-, dsaˉ-, yaˉ-, llaˉ-, maˉ-, gaꜙ- etc.) that precede it are unstressed, and their vowels reduce (a > ä). The 'acento' described in the front matter is a different thing: a contrastive ballistic accent (rapid pitch fall) that can co-occur with each of the three level tones on any syllable and is written with a dot on the tone mark.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('siempre'). The statement is made in passing in the derivational-morphology section, not in a phonology chapter; the dictionary's own phonological front matter (pp. ix-xii) treats only consonants, vowels, nine tones and tone sandhi.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the morphological word (prefix(es) + monosyllabic root, with optional person suffix fused into the root syllable); the example is the derived verb dsaˉläˉlle̱ey̱ꜘ 'to get angry'. Tone sandhi before pause (p. xii) is phrase-level and separate from stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary covers the single variety spoken in San Pedro Ozumacín, Ayotzintepec (dialect centre per Rupp 1987) and Santiago Progreso = ISO chz = ozum1235; no sub-variety is singled out and there is no separate glottocode for Ayotzintepec. Rupp 1987 notes the closest language is Palantla Chinantec (63% intelligibility).

sources.note: Front matter pp. ix-xii describes consonants, vowels, three level tones, the same tones 'con acento' (ballistic accent: pitch falls rapidly, written with a dot on the tone mark) and three rising tones, plus tone sandhi; 'acento' there means ballistic accent, not word stress. The only word-stress statement is incidental, in grammar sec. 5.1 (printed p. 254, p. 275): the basic accent of the word always falls on the last syllable, so a prefix vowel is in an unaccented position and laxes (a -> ä). Verified against the page scan.

sources.note: Sec. 3 'Tonos' (p. 5): Chinantec languages are tonal; every syllable carries a written tone; marks differ when a 'ballistic' accent falls on the syllable (realized as a rapid fall in pitch); nine tones listed. App. B (p. 8): IPA consonant/vowel inventory, ten vowel qualities, nine tones. No statement about word stress.

sources.note: Phoneme note on p. 122 (read from page scan): consonants, ten vowels (oral/nasal, short/long), three tone levels 1-3, 'The level tones may also occur with a ballistic accent, which is symbolized with an apostrophe after the tone number', and three tone glides. tone.quote: The following are the major sound shifts affecting the tone system: (1) change of vowel quantity difference to a tone (and vowel quality) difference in Oj-Pa and probably in VN-Oz. ... Tone alternations are a marker of person-number and tense-aspect in most verbs and of person-number in obligatorily possessed nouns in all Chinantec languages. ... The patterns of tone substitution are not discussed in this study. ... 6. Tone has been reconstructed on the basis of tonal data from five dialect areas: Oj-U, Tl-S, Tp-Pa, Ll-Le, and Qi-Co.
tone.locator: p. 13, ch. 2 'Phonological Developments'; p. 21 fn. 5; p. 31 'Explanatory Notes' item 6
tone.summary: Comparative dictionary: reconstructs Proto Chinantec with two tones (*H, *L; combinations *HL, *LH, *HLH) plus a ballistic accent (p. 12). For Ozumacin it only presupposes tone (length became tone 'probably in VN-Oz'; tone alternations in all Chinantec languages); Ozumacin forms lack tone marks.
